common_name: Variegated String of Hearts (Variegated Rosary Vine, Variegated Chain of Hearts)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained, gritty succulent mix in bright indirect light with some morning sun; grow only as a hanging basket or shelf container plant, since it has no cold tolerance.

directions: This sport of the standard string of hearts adds an irregular cream-white edge to each small heart-shaped leaf, and that white margin flushes pink when the plant gets a few hours of direct morning sun, giving the trailing stems a softer, more pastel look than the plain gray-green species. Because the white portions of the leaf carry no chlorophyll, this cultivar grows noticeably more slowly than unvariegated string of hearts and needs slightly brighter light to stay vigorous without reverting to plain green growth. Let the gritty, fast-draining mix dry out fully between waterings, since the tuberous stems and aerial bead-like tubers rot quickly in constantly damp soil. Trim and root stem sections in spring to propagate more plants or to fill in a thin hanging basket.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Plant Selector (Ceropegia woodii)
North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Ceropegia
general horticultural reference

common_name: Variegatum Spider Plant (Green-Center, White-Margined Spider Plant)

planting.note: Move outdoors to shade or partial shade once night temperatures stay above 50°F; in zone 9 grow outdoors April-October and bring indoors before frost. 'Variegatum' carries the opposite striping pattern of 'Vittatum' — green leaf centers edged in white margins rather than a white center stripe.

directions: Grow in shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, moderately fertile potting mix with consistent moisture; this is the original, longest-cultivated variegated spider plant selection, with each arching leaf bearing a solid green center flanked by crisp white margins along both edges — visually the reverse of the more commonly sold 'Vittatum', which reverses the color placement with a white center stripe. Like all spider plants it sends out long wiry stolons tipped with miniature plantlets that can be snipped off and rooted in water for easy propagation, and its thick, water-storing roots make it tolerant of occasional missed waterings. It is an excellent low-light performer for shaded porches and interiors where brighter, thinner-leaved foliage plants would struggle.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Chlorophytum comosum for Florida Landscapes
Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder

common_name: Ocean Spider Plant (Compact Wide-Leaf Variegated Spider Plant)

planting.note: Move outdoors to bright shade once night temperatures stay above 50°F; Ocean's broader, shorter leaves give it a tidier, more mounded shape than older spider plant selections, making it well suited to shelves, desks, and dish gardens.

directions: Ocean is a modern, more compact spider plant selection with wider, shorter, gently rippled leaves than the traditional trailing cultivars, forming a dense, tidy rosette rather than a loose, sprawling clump. Deep green leaf centers are bordered by creamy-white margins, and the plant produces the same wiry runners tipped with baby plantlets that make spider plants easy to propagate and share. It tolerates a wide range of indoor light from bright shade to filtered sun and is more forgiving of irregular watering than its lush appearance suggests, thanks to thick, fleshy storage roots. Its smaller stature fits containers and grouped displays where the larger, older spider plant cultivars would quickly outgrow the space.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Plant Selector (Chlorophytum comosum 'Ocean')
general horticultural reference

common_name: Mini White Fittonia (Dwarf White-Veined Nerve Plant)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings under high humidity or plant terrarium-grown starts in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in full shade; Mini White is a dwarf selection best suited to terrariums, bottle gardens, and dish gardens rather than open containers.

directions: Mini White is a dwarf form of the classic nerve plant, with small, closely spaced oval leaves densely netted in fine white veining over a dark green background, on a much more compact, low-growing frame than standard albivenis or the larger-leaved 'White Anne'. Its small scale and creeping habit make it a natural fit for terrariums, paludariums, and miniature dish gardens, where its extreme humidity requirement is easiest to satisfy. Like other fittonias it wilts dramatically the moment air turns dry and recovers just as quickly once humidity is restored, so open-room culture without a humidity tray, terrarium, or frequent misting rarely succeeds long-term. Keep soil evenly moist and warm, and take tip cuttings to propagate additional plantlets for filling in bare patches.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Fittonia albivenis
University of Florida IFAS Extension

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Amagris is a naturally occurring mutation of the standard never-never plant and keeps its coolest silvery tone in bright filtered light rather than deep shade.

directions: Amagris arose as a spontaneous whole-plant mutation discovered within a cultivated stand of Ctenanthe burle-marxii and was propagated onward by tissue culture for its distinctive pale, silvery-gray leaf color, which replaces the more common bright silver-and-green banding of the standard cultivar with a cooler, muted gray-green base crossed by fine dark-green herringbone striping. Leaf undersides and stems carry a plum-purple flush that shows through at the edges, adding contrast to the cool foliage tone. Like other Ctenanthe, its paddle-shaped leaves fold upright at night and relax flat by day, and the plant stays low and dense rather than tall, spreading wider than it grows upward. Bright filtered light brings out the strongest silver cast; in dimmer spots the gray-green tone flattens toward plain green even though the plant remains healthy.
sources: Foliage Factory — Ctenanthe burle-marxii 'Amagris'
Mountain Crest Gardens — Ctenanthe burle-marxii 'Amagris'

common_name: Lemon Lime Prayer Plant (Lemon Lime Maranta)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained potting mix; Lemon Lime prayer plant wants high humidity and consistent moisture and is frost-tender outside zones 10-11.

directions: Lemon Lime replaces the deep green background of the standard prayer plant with an electric blend of chartreuse, lime, and darker green in irregular herringbone-like patches, giving the foliage a brighter, almost glowing look in shaded rooms compared with the more subdued coloring of the common species and 'Fascinator'. Like other Maranta leuconeura selections its oval leaves fold upward at night and relax flat during the day, a nyctinastic movement that gives the whole plant group its common name. It is native to humid Brazilian forest floor conditions and needs consistently moist, humus-rich soil along with elevated humidity to prevent crisping leaf edges, doing best near a humidifier, pebble tray, or grouped with other moisture-loving foliage plants. Divide congested clumps when repotting in spring to propagate new plants and keep the display full.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Maranta leuconeura
general horticultural reference

common_name: Norfolk Friendship Plant (Norfolk Pilea, Pan-American Friendship Plant)

planting.note: Root 2-3 inch stem tip cuttings in moist potting mix or terrarium substrate under high humidity; Norfolk roots quickly at warm temperatures (70-75°F) and benefits from frequent pinching to stay compact rather than sprawling.

directions: Norfolk is the most heavily textured, silvery-toned selection of friendship plant commonly sold, with deeply quilted oval leaves that emerge reddish-pink before settling into a metallic silver-green surface crossed by dark charcoal-green veins, the undersides flushed burgundy-red. The pronounced puckering and metallic sheen make Norfolk's foliage stand out more than the plain species or the chartreuse-toned 'Moon Valley' selection under the same bright indirect light. As with other friendship plants, stems root readily from cuttings within days under warm, humid conditions, which is how it earned its common name as a plant endlessly shared between growers. Pinch stem tips regularly to keep growth dense and low, since older stems become woody and sparse after a year or two and are best replaced from fresh cuttings.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Plant Selector (Pilea involucrata 'Norfolk')
North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Pilea involucrata

common_name: Chopin Peace Lily (Compact Classic Peace Lily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in deep to moderate shade; Chopin stays noticeably more compact than 'Mauna Loa' or standard peace lily, making it a better fit for smaller tabletop and desk containers.

directions: Chopin is a compact, classic peace lily selection bred for a tidy, upright habit that never grows as large as 'Mauna Loa' or other big-growing peace lily cultivars, making it easier to place on desks, shelves, and smaller shaded tables. Glossy, dark green lance-shaped leaves surround the plant's simple white spathe-and-spadix flowers, which appear intermittently through the year given adequate warmth and humidity. Like other peace lilies it tolerates low indoor light and irregular watering better than most houseplants, wilting visibly when thirsty and recovering quickly once watered, though consistently letting it dry out too far will scorch leaf tips over time. Keep it out of reach of pets, since the foliage is toxic to cats and dogs if chewed.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Plant Selector (Spathiphyllum 'Chopin')
University of Florida IFAS Extension

common_name: Helen Lewis Rex Begonia (Classic Purple-Black Silver-Banded Rex Begonia)

planting.note: Grow year-round as a houseplant or shaded patio container plant in bright, indirect light; move outdoors to a shaded spot for summer only after night temperatures stay reliably above 50°F.

directions: Hybridized before 1947 and still widely grown, Helen Lewis is one of the oldest and most enduring named Rex begonia cultivars, having received the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for its reliable performance. Its oval leaves show a wide silver-gray band ringed on both sides by purple-black, with a faint pink flush at the color transitions, a more restrained and elegant color scheme than the brighter, busier patterns of many modern Rex hybrids. As with other Rex begonias, it needs a shallow pot, porous, well-drained mix, and consistently high humidity to prevent leaf-edge browning, and it is generally considered one of the easier-to-grow cultivars in this famously fussy group. Divide the rhizome at repotting time to produce new plants, and keep it out of direct sun, which fades and scorches the delicate leaf coloring.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Begonia 'Helen Lewis' (Award of Garden Merit)
American Begonia Society — Rex Cultorum Begonias reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Maria Allusion colors most vividly with bright indirect light and is frost-tender outside zones 10-11.

directions: Part of the same commercially bred Allusion series as 'Berry Allusion' and 'Pink Allusion' already grown for the pink-to-green color transition of their arrow-shaped leaves, Maria Allusion opens with young foliage that is almost entirely pink with copper undertones before gradually maturing to green accented with reddish-purple veins radiating from the midrib. This shift from vivid pink new growth to a subtler green-and-copper mature leaf gives a single plant a two-stage look that changes noticeably as it grows. It holds a compact, self-heading rosette habit while young and begins to vine and climb with age, doing best trained onto a small moss pole or stake at that stage. Provide bright indirect light and humidity above 50 percent for the strongest color, and keep it away from pets, since the sap contains irritating calcium oxalate crystals.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Syngonium podophyllum
International Aroid Society reference

common_name: Snow Queen Pothos (Heavily White Variegated Pothos)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained potting mix in bright indirect light; Snow Queen carries even heavier white variegation than 'Marble Queen' and needs bright light to avoid reverting toward plain green.

directions: Snow Queen is among the most heavily variegated pothos cultivars in cultivation, with leaves that run mostly cream-white and only lightly flecked with green, making it noticeably paler overall than the marbled green-and-white pattern of 'Marble Queen'. Because so much of the leaf surface lacks chlorophyll, Snow Queen grows more slowly and stays smaller and less vigorous than other Epipremnum aureum selections, and it needs consistently bright, indirect light to sustain what little green pigment it has without stalling out. It trails or climbs in the same manner as other pothos and tolerates average indoor humidity and occasional missed waterings, but is more prone to reverting to greener growth than lightly variegated selections if light is too low. Trim any all-green reversion shoots promptly to keep the plant's white character.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Epipremnum aureum
general horticultural reference

planting.note: Divide offsets from the base in spring or early summer when repotting into fresh, well-drained mix; Siam Aurora's red coloring intensifies in brighter light but the plant still performs acceptably in low-light interiors.

directions: Siam Aurora was bred specifically to push red pigment further than any wild Aglaonema species achieves on its own, and the result is a bushy, upright plant with glossy, lance-shaped leaves marbled in pink, green, and red, carried on matching pink-flushed stems with bright red midribs. This modern hybrid brought vivid red-and-pink foliage color into the mainstream houseplant trade and remains one of the most recognizable colored Aglaonema cultivars sold today. It holds its color best with bright, indirect light but, like other Aglaonema, tolerates considerably lower light than most colorful foliage plants, simply with somewhat less intense variegation. Let the top inch or two of potting mix dry before watering again, since overwatering is a bigger risk than underwatering, and keep it above 60°F and away from cold drafts.
sources: Gardenia.net — Aglaonema 'Siam Aurora'
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Aglaonema production guide

planting.note: Move outdoors to a shaded location after temperatures remain reliably above 55°F; in zone 9 place outdoors April-October and overwinter indoors. Corona needs consistently high humidity and filtered or rainwater to avoid brown leaf edges.

directions: Corona is named for the way its coloring radiates outward like a halo, with a pale rose-and-silver center fading through concentric bands of green toward a dark green leaf edge and a reddish midrib running down the center, on broad, nearly rounded leaves distinct from the narrower, more elongated foliage of many other roseopicta selections. It is one of the most widely grown named calathea cultivars in the trade, prized for that gradient banding effect as much as for the classic nightly leaf-folding movement shared by all prayer plants. It needs moderate to bright indirect light, since direct sun quickly scorches the delicate pink and silver tones, along with consistently moist, humus-rich soil and humidity above 50 percent. Water with distilled water or rainwater when possible, since this cultivar is notably sensitive to the fluoride and dissolved salts found in most tap water.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Calathea roseopicta
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Calathea and Goeppertia Species for Florida

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Tricolor holds its striping with less direct light than the more color-intense 'Colorama' selection.

directions: Tricolor is the older, more subdued striped form of the classic Madagascar dragon tree, with narrow, arching leaves showing a genuinely three-part color scheme of green margins, a central cream or white stripe, and a fine pink edge running along the outermost rim, giving a more evenly distributed and understated variegation than the bolder pink-and-cream 'Colorama'. It develops the same slow-growing, multi-trunked, sculptural silhouette typical of Dracaena marginata over years, making it a long-lived architectural specimen in a floor container even under fairly modest indoor light. Water only after the top inch or two of potting mix has dried, since dracaenas are far more prone to root rot from overwatering than to drought stress, and use filtered or distilled water when possible to avoid the tan leaf-tip burn that fluoride causes over time. Keep it away from cold drafts and temperatures below about 55°F, since it has no frost tolerance.
sources: Gardenia.net — Dracaena marginata 'Tricolor'
